segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, in keeping with the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am grateful to God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as my ancestors did, as I constantly remember you in my prayers, night and day,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: longing to see you, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, a faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and, I am convinced, lives in you as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for God did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but of power and love and self-discipline.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, or of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the good news, by the power of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace. This grace was given to us in Christ Jesus before the long ages began,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but has now been revealed through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this good news I was appointed herald and apostle and teacher.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason I also suffer these things. But I am not ashamed, for I know the one I have trusted, and I am convinced that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Hold to the pattern of sound words that you heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Guard the good thing entrusted to you, through the Holy Spirit who lives in us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You know this, that everyone in Asia has turned away from me, among them Phygelus and Hermogenes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: on the contrary, when he came to Rome he searched hard for me and found me—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day—and how much service he gave in Ephesus, you know very well.

notes.note: The phrase stands between two clauses and can attach to either: Paul remembers Timothy in his prayers night and day, or he longs night and day to see him. The English keeps the phrase at the same point, so both readings stay open.

The traditional 'spirit of fear' suggests fear in general, and 'timidity' suggests shyness. In Greek usage this word is the regular term for cowardice, the failure of nerve that makes someone shrink from danger or duty. It is distinct from the ordinary word for fear, which can be a good thing. The charge not to be ashamed in the next verse fits this stronger sense.

Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so this may be a disposition God gives ('a spirit of power') or the Holy Spirit himself ('the Spirit, who produces power'). Most translations print a lower-case 'spirit', and that is followed here. Many interpreters think the Holy Spirit, named in verse 14, is in view.

The word occurs only here in the New Testament. It belongs to a family of words for sober good sense and moderation, and it can mean either the exercise of self-control or sound, level-headed judgment. Older versions have 'a sound mind'; most modern ones have 'self-control' or 'self-discipline'.

'Gospel' has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

notes.traditional: before the world began; before times eternal; before the ages began
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'before age-long times', the adjective usually translated 'eternal' joined to the plural 'times'. 'Before eternal times' makes little sense in English, so the phrase is rendered as the long ages of the world's history, with God's grace given before they began. The same expression occurs in Romans 16:25 and Titus 1:2.

In the wider Greek world this word was used for the visible manifestation of a god coming to help, and for the arrival or accession of a ruler. 'Savior' was likewise a title given to gods and emperors. A first-century reader would have heard both words as claiming for Jesus honours that others claimed for themselves. Elsewhere in these letters the word usually refers to Christ's future coming; here it refers to his first.

Many manuscripts read 'teacher of the Gentiles', and older English versions follow them. The shorter reading is printed in the SBLGNT. The longer one is widely regarded as an addition drawn from the parallel in 1 Timothy 2:7.

notes.phrase: what I have entrusted to him
notes.traditional: that which I have committed unto him
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'my deposit', a legal term for property left in someone's safekeeping. It can mean what Paul has entrusted to God (his life, his work, his future) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the message, as in verse 14, where Timothy is to guard 'the good deposit'). Most translations take it the first way, as here. A substantial number of scholars prefer the second because of verse 14.

This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. It is not the continent. 'Everyone' is probably a broad statement of general desertion rather than a literal count. Nothing further is known of Phygelus and Hermogenes.

Paul prays for Onesiphorus's household now and for Onesiphorus himself 'on that day', and he greets only the household in 4:19. Many interpreters conclude that Onesiphorus had died. Others think he was simply away from home. The text does not say, and the question bears on later debates about prayer for the dead.

notes.phrase: may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord
notes.note: 'Lord' occurs twice, and it is unclear whether both refer to the same person. One common reading takes the first as Christ and the second as God the Father, the judge on the last day. Others take the doubling as a fixed form of prayer. The Greek also plays on 'found' in verse 17: Onesiphorus found Paul, and Paul prays that he may find mercy.

candidates.reason: It recurs across Luke-Acts, Paul, Hebrews and Revelation, and translators split between 'serve' and 'worship', which obscures that it denotes cultic service to a deity.
It recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians, the Pastorals and 1 Peter, where 'gift', 'spiritual gift' and 'grace-gift' compete and the link to χάρις is easily lost.
It is used in 2 Thessalonians and throughout the Pastorals for Christ's first and future coming, and 'appearing', 'manifestation' and 'coming' should not vary at random.
The noun and its verb κηρύσσω and κήρυγμα need one decision between the 'preach/preacher' family and the 'proclaim/herald' family across the whole New Testament.
The health metaphor ('sound' or 'healthy' teaching and words) is a recurring motif of the Pastorals and needs one consistent rendering.
